statement: In observational samples of people who used cannabis regularly or had a cannabis use disorder, the share with cannabis withdrawal, as each study defined it, differed greatly by where the samples came from, in a 2020 meta-analysis of 50 cohorts with 23,518 participants (searched to June 2019; Bahji et al., 2020; AMSTAR 2 critically low; English only; no group of people who did not cut down for comparison): 17 in 100 (95% CI 13 to 22) in 15 general-population samples holding 17,475 people, 54 in 100 (48 to 59) in 28 outpatient samples (5,684 people) and 87 in 100 (79 to 94) in 7 inpatient or residential samples (357 people). Withdrawal at any time in life was reported far more often than withdrawal in the past year (76 in 100, 70 to 82, in 18 cohorts, against 31 in 100, 27 to 36, in 32); like the differences by setting, these are comparisons between groups of studies, not within the same people. The one general-population sample assessed with DSM-5 criteria found it in 12.1% of 1,527 people. The review's headline figure, 47 in 100 (41 to 52; I2 99.2%; cohorts from 8% to 100%), is close to the plain average of the cohort estimates and is driven by small clinical samples; counted by participants it is about 28 in 100 (the review's own count, 6,469 of 23,518, is 27.5%, editors' calculation, and its forest plot's fixed-effect total, which gives larger cohorts more weight, is 0.28). Men and women did not differ (27 and 26 in 100, 15 studies), although the review's conclusions say withdrawal was more common in men. In DSM-5, as two reviews summarise it, cannabis withdrawal means at least three of seven symptoms developing within about a week after heavy and prolonged use stops (Bahji et al., 2020, which also word it as within 7 days of reduced use; Connor et al., 2021): irritability, anger or aggression; nervousness or anxiety; sleep difficulty; less appetite or weight loss; restlessness; low mood; and a physical symptom such as headache, sweating or stomach pain, with distress or impairment that Connor et al. describe as clinically severe. Many of these symptoms also occur in withdrawal from other substances and in other mental disorders (Connor et al., 2021). As described in narrative reviews, whose figures are second-hand, symptoms typically begin 1 to 2 days after stopping, peak within the first week (at 2 to 6 days in one account) and fade within 1 to 2 weeks (Curran et al., 2016; Connor et al., 2021), while a 2020 professional statement describes a longer course, beginning a few days after stopping or cutting down, peaking at about 10 days and ending after 30 days (Page et al., 2020); craving, nightmares and nausea are also prominent (Curran et al., 2016), and irritability, sleep difficulty, low mood, craving and anxiety are listed by Volkow et al. (2014); people seeking help to stop report symptoms that include anxiety, sleep problems, appetite disturbance and low mood (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009), which a later review by the same first author calls the most common symptoms, often severe enough to impair everyday life (Hall, 2015); one review gives around half of people who use daily as having withdrawal when they stop, citing an earlier review (Curran et al., 2016). On medical risk the sources disagree without evidence: one review says that, in people without other medical or psychiatric illness, withdrawal does not pose serious risks and usually needs only supportive care (Connor et al., 2021), while the 2020 professional statement advises clinicians to tell people who use heavily over the long term not to stop suddenly because of the risk of withdrawal (Page et al., 2020); neither cites a study for this. In one laboratory study, oral THC given by the researchers eased the symptoms (Budney et al., 2007, as cited by Curran et al., 2016), and in trials the THC medicines dronabinol and nabiximols reduced withdrawal symptoms but did not reduce cannabis use compared with a placebo (Curran et al., 2016). Sleep after stopping is covered in more detail in the claims on sleep. The cohorts defined regular use differently, most predate DSM-5, the review took the lowest threshold where studies offered several, cohorts with more tobacco use reported more withdrawal (a comparison between studies), and in people who use both daily, stopping both gives stronger symptoms than stopping either alone (Curran et al., 2016). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: When people who use cannabis regularly stop or cut down, some get withdrawal: irritability or anger, nervousness, poor sleep, less appetite, restlessness, low mood, or physical symptoms such as headaches. A 2020 review found it in about 17 in 100 people with regular use in general-population surveys, 54 in 100 in outpatient groups and 87 in 100 in inpatient groups; withdrawal at any time in life was reported much more often than in the past year. Reviews say it usually starts 1 to 2 days after stopping, is worst in the first week and fades within 1 to 2 weeks, though one professional statement says it can last about a month. Expert sources disagree on whether it carries any medical risk, and none gives evidence for its view. The studies defined regular use and withdrawal in different ways, many of the same feelings also come with other conditions, and none checked how often they occur in people who do not cut down.
population: People with regular cannabis use or a cannabis use disorder in 50 observational cohorts (15 general-population, 28 outpatient, 7 inpatient or residential; 38 from North America), and people seeking help to stop, as described in narrative reviews
exposure: Stopping or cutting down after regular use (regular use as each cohort defined it; the review gives no common definition)
comparator: None (prevalence without a comparison group); settings and timeframes compared with each other
outcome: Cannabis withdrawal syndrome as each study defined and measured it (rating scales, checklists and diagnostic interviews; most cohorts used DSM-III-R or DSM-IV criteria for the use disorder), at any time in life or in the past year; symptoms and time course as described in reviews
magnitude: Bahji 2020, random-effects pooled prevalence: general population 17% (95% CI 13 to 22 in Table 2; 13 to 21 in the text; 15 cohorts; 17,475 people; I2 98%); outpatient 54% (48 to 59; 28; 5,684); inpatient 87% (79 to 94; 7; 357 in the text, 359 in Figure 2); past year 31% (27 to 36; 32 cohorts); lifetime 76% (70 to 82; 18); overall 47% (41 to 52 in the abstract, 27 to 37 in the Results text; I2 99.2%; range 8% to 100%); Figure 2 totals: random effects 0.46 (0.37 to 0.55), fixed effect 0.28 (0.27 to 0.28); men 27% (21 to 34), women 26% (19 to 33), P = .99; one DSM-5 population cohort 12.1% of 1,527. Participant count: 6,469 of 23,518 in the abstract (27.5%, editors' calculation; cohort sizes times prevalences in Table 1 sum to 6,470). Time course as described in reviews: onset 1-2 days (24-48 hours), peak within the first week (2-6 days), resolution within 1-2 weeks; in one professional statement, onset after a few days, peak at about 10 days, end after 30 days.

evidence.locator: Diagnosis, screening and prevention › Diagnostic systems, 3rd paragraph; Management › Cannabis withdrawal, 1st-2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: DSM-5 withdrawal in the Primer's words: three or more signs within 1 week of cessation (irritability, anger or aggression; nervousness or anxiety; sleep difficulty; decreased appetite or weight loss; restlessness; depressed mood; at least one physical symptom causing severe discomfort, such as abdominal pain, shakiness, sweating, fever, chills or headache), which must cause clinically severe distress or impairment (the Primer's wording; reduced use is not mentioned). Many of these symptoms also occur in other substance withdrawal or in other mental disorders. Second-hand: symptoms typically begin 24-48 hours after stopping, peak within the first week and last 1-2 weeks (Budney et al., 2003); 12% of people who use frequently had DSM-5 withdrawal in the past 12 months in a US national sample (Livne et al., 2019). In Management, figures cited to Livne et al. and Bahji et al. together (refs 177 and 203) are relabelled as 12-17% in the general population of people who use cannabis and as 54% of outpatients and 87% of inpatients with a use disorder seeking treatment reporting clinically severe withdrawal. Without medical or psychiatric comorbidity, withdrawal is said not to pose serious risks, with most people needing only supportive care, in a sentence that cites no source.

evidence.locator: Cannabis addiction and withdrawal, 2nd paragraph (p. 299); References 71 to 73 and 77 (p. 304)
evidence.extracted: Second-hand: a withdrawal syndrome said to affect around 50% of people who use daily when they stop, typically beginning 1-2 days after stopping, peaking at 2-6 days and fading by 1-2 weeks (ref 71, a 2004 review by Budney and colleagues); prominent symptoms craving, sleep problems, nightmares, anger, irritability, dysphoria and nausea (ref 72, Allsop and colleagues, 2011); symptoms can be alleviated by THC in a dose-dependent way (ref 73, by its title a study of oral THC suppressing cannabis withdrawal symptoms, Budney et al., 2007); in people who use cannabis and tobacco daily, combined withdrawal is stronger than withdrawal from either alone (ref 77).
evidence.check_note: Adjudication (AI reader 243, 2026-10-31): the title of ref 73 (oral THC; Budney et al., 2007) added from p. 304, as second reader 213 noted, and the source's verb (alleviated) restored; the other content unchanged.

evidence.locator: Health effects of cannabis › Chronic effects, 3rd paragraph (p. 1386); Reference 40 (p. 1390)
evidence.extracted: Second-hand: people seeking help to stop report withdrawal symptoms including anxiety, insomnia, appetite disturbance and depression (ref 40, Budney & Hughes, 2006); tolerance to many effects of THC develops in animals and humans, and a cannabinoid-receptor blocker brings on a withdrawal syndrome in rats, mice and dogs that THC reverses.

Second-hand: the evidence for a withdrawal syndrome is said to have strengthened since 1993; people who seek help often report symptoms that make abstinence harder, most commonly anxiety, insomnia, appetite disturbance and depression (ref 44, Budney & Hughes, 2006), often severe enough to impair everyday functioning (ref 45, Allsop and colleagues, 2012); a double-blind trial found the symptoms markedly reduced by a cannabis extract (ref 46, nabiximols, 2014).

risk_of_bias.note: Cohorts mostly rated fair (36 of 50) or poor (12) on the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale; clinical and residential samples selected for heavy use; lifetime withdrawal recalled in surveys; the lowest available threshold used; no comparison group to subtract background symptoms; the review is AMSTAR 2 critically low (card sc_bahji_2020).

inconsistency.note: I2 99.2% overall and 98% within general-population samples, whose estimates run from 7.6% to 34.4%; two analyses of one national survey gave 8.0% and 34.4%. Setting and timeframe explain part of the spread, not all.

indirectness.note: Regular use undefined; most definitions predate DSM-5; the pools include a prison survey and a synthetic-cannabinoid detoxification sample; the symptom description and time course are second-hand (narrative reviews and a professional statement), and these sources differ on the time course (1 to 2 weeks against about 30 days).

imprecision.note: The setting estimates have intervals a few points wide.

publication_bias.note: Tests reported as negative (supplement not read); of little meaning for prevalence estimates.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim (prevalence in the populations sampled): starts low; down one level each for risk of bias, inconsistency and indirectness: very low. The headline 47% is not used as the answer, because it averages cohorts of very different kinds and tracks the average cohort rather than the average participant (card sc_bahji_2020; the review's own fixed-effect total is 0.28); the setting-specific figures are. The narrative reviews describe symptoms and time course second-hand and overlap with the meta-analysis (Connor et al., 2021, take their 54% and 87% from it, relabelled), so they are not counted as further studies. Status replicated: in 50 cohorts from many teams withdrawal was found in some people who used regularly, consistently more often in clinical samples; how often varies widely, which the inconsistency rating carries.
